pharm: A salicylanilide anthelmintic active against intestinal tapeworms. It is poorly absorbed from the gut, so it acts locally on the scolex and proximal segments of the worm. It is a taenicide rather than a taenifuge - the worm is killed and passed in a partly digested form rather than expelled intact.
quick: 2 g chewed as a single dose (single-dose tapeworms); H. nana needs a 7-day course
Take after a light breakfast; chew tablets then swallow with water
Considered acceptable when treatment needed (poorly absorbed); no contraindication noted
Stool clearance of worm/scolex; for T. solium, anti-emetic and purgative considerations
summary: Niclosamide is an oral anthelmintic used to treat intestinal tapeworm (cestode) infections - beef tapeworm (Taenia saginata), pork tapeworm (Taenia solium), fish tapeworm (Diphyllobothrium latum), and dwarf tapeworm (Hymenolepis nana). It is on the WHO List of Essential Medicines but is NOT currently marketed in the United States (it has been discontinued there), so US prescribing data are limited and the information here is drawn from WHO, EMA, and BNF sources. It is poorly absorbed and acts locally in the gut, killing the worm so it is passed in digested fragments. Single-dose therapy treats most tapeworms; H. nana requires a 7-day course. It does not kill ova, so it is ineffective against the larval/cysticercosis stage of T. solium.

admin: Give after a light breakfast (not on a completely empty stomach for taeniasis regimens)
Chew the tablets thoroughly, or crush them for young children, then swallow with a little water
If vomiting is a concern, the single 2 g dose may be split into two halves taken 1 hour apart
For T. solium, consider an antiemetic beforehand and a saline purgative about 2 hours after the dose to clear the bowel of disintegrated proglottids and ova
Eradication is confirmed by absence of eggs/proglottids in stool over the following weeks; the scolex is often digested and not recovered intact
moa: Niclosamide is a salicylanilide that acts directly on the tapeworm. It uncouples oxidative phosphorylation in the mitochondria of the cestode and inhibits anaerobic ATP production (and glucose/oxygen uptake), depriving the worm of energy. This kills the scolex and proximal segments on contact within the intestinal lumen. Because it is very poorly absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, its action is essentially confined to the gut and there is minimal systemic exposure. It is a taenicide (kills the worm in place, which is then passed partially digested) rather than a taenifuge (does not expel the worm intact), and it has no effect on tapeworm ova.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to niclosamide or any component
relative: Treatment of T. solium without measures to prevent vomiting/egg dispersal (theoretical cysticercosis risk)
It is NOT effective against systemic larval infection (neurocysticercosis) - use appropriate alternative therapy
monitor: Stool examination for clearance of eggs/proglottids after treatment

preg: Because niclosamide is poorly absorbed and acts locally in the gut, systemic exposure is minimal and it is generally regarded as acceptable when treatment of tapeworm infection is needed; no specific contraindication in pregnancy is noted in WHO/MSF guidance. As with any drug in pregnancy, use only when clearly indicated. (Not FDA-evaluated; data from WHO/EMA/BNF.)
lact: Owing to negligible systemic absorption, niclosamide is considered compatible with breastfeeding and no contraindication during lactation is noted in WHO/MSF guidance. (Data from WHO/EMA/BNF.)
renal: No dose adjustment is expected in renal impairment because niclosamide is minimally absorbed and acts within the gut lumen rather than relying on renal elimination.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is described for hepatic impairment, again reflecting the drug's negligible systemic absorption.

minor: Clinically significant systemic drug interactions are unlikely because of minimal absorption
interactions.food: Take after a light breakfast; tablets are chewed/crushed and swallowed with water.
interactions.alcohol: Alcohol should be avoided during treatment.

emergency: Severe allergic reaction (rash, swelling, difficulty breathing)

monitoring: Stool examination for tapeworm eggs/proglottids to confirm cure (e.g. several weeks after treatment)
For H. nana, ensure the full 7-day course is completed
For T. solium, vigilance for measures preventing egg dispersal
counsel: Chew the tablets well (or crush them for children) and swallow with a little water, taken after a light breakfast
Take the single dose for most tapeworms; for dwarf tapeworm you must take it daily for a full week
You may not see a whole worm passed - the medicine usually breaks it up before it leaves the body
Mild stomach upset, nausea, or loose stools can occur and are usually short-lived
Avoid alcohol while you are taking it
Maintain careful hand and food hygiene to avoid re-infection, and have a follow-up stool test as advised

pearls: Not currently FDA-marketed (discontinued in the US) - clinical data here are drawn from WHO, EMA and BNF sources
WHO Essential Medicine and a first-line luminal taenicide for intestinal tapeworms
Poorly absorbed - acts locally; minimal systemic toxicity, drug interactions, or organ-impairment dosing concerns
Taenicide not taenifuge: the worm is passed partly digested, so the scolex is often not recovered intact
Ineffective against tapeworm ova and against larval T. solium (cysticercosis) - does not treat neurocysticercosis
For T. solium, give an antiemetic and a purgative to reduce the theoretical risk of egg regurgitation and autoinfection
Praziquantel is the more commonly used alternative where niclosamide is unavailable
missed: For single-dose tapeworm treatment there is no missed dose. For the 7-day dwarf-tapeworm (H. nana) course, if a daily dose is missed take it as soon as you remember the same day; if it is nearly time for the next day's dose, skip it and continue - do not double up. Complete the full week.
overdose: Because niclosamide is very poorly absorbed, systemic toxicity from overdose is unlikely. Excess may cause gastrointestinal upset (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea). There is no specific antidote; management is supportive, and a prompt laxative with fluid replacement may be used to clear the gut.
